newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ says Bougainville/PNG talks moving positively.
newsitem.headline: NZ says Bougainville/PNG talks moving positively.

text.p: New Zealand on Friday gave a positive progress report from the first week of peace talks it is hosting for rival factions in a nine-year secessionist war on Papua New Guinea's Bougainville Island.
Foreign Minister Don McKinnon told reporters after a visit to the forum at Burnham Military Camp, near the South Island city of Christchurch, that the parties had settled down to serious talks.

He said he had spoken for about an hour with rebel Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA) leader Joseph Kabui and the Papua New Guinea-backed Bougainville Transitional Government's (BTG) Premier Gerard Sinato and both had given him a positive message.
"Sinato and Kabui said to me they are really seeing daylight in the discussions now in terms of the kinds of processes they believe will be productive in the long run," he said.

McKinnon's message to the group, now numbering some 60 delegates and growing as more arrive, was that there was no time limit on their talks. He said he would meet them again next week for another update.
"I'm determined that they get the opportunity to put down a very good, strong foundation and I'm satisfied that what they've achieved so far... (means) we're certainly on the right track."
But he added: "There is no quick fix here", noting that the main issues, such as the role of the Papua New Guinea defence force, had been key for 10 years.

Thousands have died in the Bougainville conflict since landowners revolted in 1988 over environmental damage caused by the huge Panguna copper mine, and the royalties they received from it. The mine is owned by a unit of the Anglo-Australian giant RTZ Corp.
New Zealand is providing logistical support for the talks but is not an official participant. The forum involves only representatives of the island and Papua New Guinea is not taking part.
McKinnon said he was encouraging the Bougainvillean group to go through local issues, "to reach a point where they can in all confidence actively engage with the PNG government".
But he characterised the next step as "a kind of agreement to a process which will last for quite a while".
The minister said the talks were overlapping with a time of political uncertainty in Papua New Guinea after elections that ended last week and signalled a new government.
"It will be very much the make-up of the government, the make-up of the coalition...which will determine where to from here.
"But given the discussions I have had with quite a wide range of PNG leaders, I sense there is a renewed determination to get this conflict behind them," he told a news conference.
As McKinnon visited, another nine delegates were expected to join the discussion group which has already swelled from an initial 50 at last Saturday's launch.
Of those due to arrive through Friday and Saturday four represent the BRA, or its Bougainville Interim Government (BIG) political arm, and are travelling via the Solomon Islands.
The others were linked to the BTG and were coming from Bougainville's small offshore island of Buka, officials said.

McKinnon said he understood there had been some discussions about creating a neutral zone on the island. Sources at the talks have said one aim is to seek a zone policed by a Pacific peacekeeping force where substantive peace negotiations can take place.
